correctness.rationale: In a complete multipartite graph, a selected vertex in part \(i\) has exactly \(q-c_i\) neighbours outside \(D\), so certification is precisely the exclusion of value one. A set dominates exactly when it meets at least two parts or is one whole part, giving the ordinary domination polynomial used in the formula. Among dominating sets, every \(q=1\) set is a certification failure, contributing \(Nz^{N-1}\). For \(q\ge2\), the bad event for part \(i\) is: omit exactly one vertex outside \(V_i\) and a nonempty proper subset inside \(V_i\); pairwise intersections are possible only at \(q=2\), with one omitted vertex in each of two parts of size at least two, and triple intersections are impossible. Inclusion--exclusion therefore gives exactly the displayed correction terms. An independent brute-force enumeration over all 58 complete multipartite part profiles of total order at most 8 matched the closed formula coefficient-by-coefficient.
correctness.risk: The formula assumes at least two nonempty parts; disconnected/one-part degenerate cases need separate conventions.

value.rationale: The result gives an all-set polynomial for a canonical graph class and turns certification into a sharp part-occupancy rule. It strictly generalizes the existing \(K_{3,n}\) calculation and is directly reusable for coefficients, totals and specializations across arbitrary multipartite profiles.
value.risk: The inclusion--exclusion proof is elementary once the exact half-shadow condition is written in omission coordinates.

final_claim: For \(G=K_{n_1,\ldots,n_r}\), a dominating set \(D\) with omission counts \(c_i=n_i-|D\cap V_i|\) and total \(q=|V\setminus D|\) is certified exactly when \(q-c_i\ne1\) for every occupied part. Combining this with the domination criterion yields the stated closed certified-domination polynomial for arbitrary part sizes, extending the previously known \(K_{3,n}\) formulas.
limitations: The theorem is specific to complete multipartite graphs and does not address certified domination polynomials under graph operations or more general perfect graph classes.
